en: The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Elder Luṣi*, translated by an unknown person and now appended to the Eastern Jin catalog:
"If one clings to stinginess and greed, one will be despised by humans and devas; therefore, the wise should practice giving."

Why is this so? I have heard that in the past there was a great householder named Lu-zhi, whose family was immensely wealthy with immeasurable assets; his storehouses were overflowing like those of Vaiśravaṇa. This was because, in former times, he cultivated the cause of giving toward supreme fields of merit, and thus obtained this retribution.
However, when giving, they were unable to do so with a sincere heart; for this reason, although they were wealthy, their disposition was always base and inferior.
The clothes they wore were soiled and impure;
as for what they ate, they filled their hunger with a mixture of grains, weeds, tares, sorrel, beans, grasses, and vegetables.
They use vinegar, dregs, air, or water to quench their thirst;
they ride in dilapidated, old carts with roofs made of woven grass and leaves;

regarding their own wealth and possessions, they give rise to stinginess, exhausting their spirits and laboring their minds to guard them diligently, suffering weariness and toil in their management, like servants who are mocked by all people.
At that time, Rāhula spoke these verses:
"The causes of giving differ, And the fruits received vary accordingly.
When the gift of faith is offered with deep sincerity, The reward obtained is as vast as one's own heart's desire."
"If one does not harbor a sense of earnest reverence, giving in vain yields no pure reward;
though Lu-zhi was immensely wealthy, his contemptuous behavior led to ridicule.

Furthermore, on another occasion during a city festival, the houses were magnificently adorned, decorated with colorful paintings, and hung with silk banners and canopies. Every place was surrounded by lapis lazuli ornaments, flower crowns were suspended, and fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground. Exquisite flowers were arrayed, and the windows, lattices, and doors were embellished with floral decorations. Each dwelling featured various kinds of music, song, dance, and amusements, where they enjoyed themselves in delight as if in the palaces of the devas.

At all the gates, golden vases were filled with fragrant water; throughout the streets and alleys, silk banners and canopies were suspended, various famous flowers were strewn about, and fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground.
At that time, Luṣi saw the various people gathered together, dancing and playing to their hearts' content, and he thought to himself:
"Even slaves, beggars, and those of low station are all wearing borrowed clothes and eating fine food;
I now have sufficient clothing, necklaces, and wealth of my own—why do I not enjoy myself?"
He hurried home, took the key himself, opened the door of the storehouse, and after taking five coins, he closed and locked the door again. He then thought to himself:
"If I eat at my own home now, it will not suffice for my mother, wife, and kinsmen;
yet if I go to another's house, there may be a host or a beggar who comes to me and asks for alms."

Thereupon, he used two coins to buy flour, two coins to purchase wine, and one coin to buy scallions; taking salt wrapped in the lapel of his garment from his own home, he carried it out beyond the city walls and headed toward the foot of a tree.

Having arrived beneath the tree, he saw many crows; thinking that if he remained there, the crows would come to peck and snatch at him, he immediately went to a cemetery. There he saw various dogs, so he fled once more to a secluded and quiet place.
He placed salt in wine and mixed it with parched grain and onions to eat.
Although he had not drunk wine before, he became instantly and greatly intoxicated.
Once he was thoroughly intoxicated, he spoke these words:
"The entire kingdom is immediately making great celebration; why am I alone not celebrating?
He then began to dance and sang aloud, his lyrics saying:
"Even if Śakra himself were to celebrate today, He would still not equal my joy."
"How much more so Vaiśravaṇa? He further said:
"Now, on this festive occasion, I indulge in wine and great merriment; I surpass Vaiśravaṇa and even excel Śakra, the Lord of Devas."
"Śakra-devānām-indra, together with countless hosts of devas, was on his way to Jetavana. Along the road, he saw this Luṭi, who was both intoxicated and dancing, singing that he surpassed Śakra."
Śakra silently thought:
"This stingy and greedy man drinks wine in a secluded place and insults me.
He then further thought:
"I must not go to the Buddha's presence now; I shall trouble him first.
Śakra-devānām-indra then transformed his body to resemble Lu-zhi and went straight to his house. He gathered the parents, servants, and kinsmen, sat before his mother, and said to her:
"Listen to my loving words!"

"In the past and present, a great spirit of stinginess has followed me, which causes me to be so parsimonious that I do not eat, nor do I give money, wealth, or treasures to my parents or my kinsmen; all this is due to that spirit of stinginess."
Today, as I was traveling, I encountered a practitioner who bestowed a potent mantra upon me, enabling me to eliminate the spirit of stinginess;
even if that spirit of stinginess should ever return, it will never again be able to disturb or trouble me.
However, this ghost of stinginess resembles me; if it should come, the gatekeepers will surely strike it painfully with their clubs.
It will certainly feign, saying: "I am Lu-zhi."
"None of his family members believed his words.
He opened the storehouses wide, brought out various treasures, and prepared fine food and drink; he then caused his mother, wife, and kinsmen to all be fully satiated."
When the meal was finished, he said to the gatekeeper:

"Close the gates quickly! Should the spirit of stinginess happen to arrive, wait until I have distributed the necklaces, bestowed the garments upon all, and performed various musical performances; only then may you open the gates."
"Immediately, he opened the treasury wide; first, he gave exquisite necklaces to his mother, next to his wife, and then distributed them throughout all the men and women within the house.
To the guests who had come from outside, he likewise gave necklaces, as well as food, clothing, and drink, and performed various kinds of music."
The members of his household smeared their bodies with various fragrant perfumes and burned black aloeswood incense.
At that time, Śakra took his mother by one hand and led his wife by the other; they danced with joy, indulging in pleasures and amusements beyond description.
When the people of Śrāvastī heard that the stingy spirit had been exorcised from the householder Luṭi, they all gathered together and came to see it.

When Luṭi awoke from his intoxication and returned to the city, he went straight to his own home. Seeing the crowds of people filling his doorway and hearing the sounds of singing and dancing within the house, he was utterly astonished and thought to himself:
"Is it not the case that the King, out of anger toward me, has brought his ministers and a great assembly of troops to my house, intending to execute me?"
"Is it because the people of Śrāvastī have gathered for a festival that they have all entered my house?
Or is it because these devas, wishing to increase my merit, have come to my house and performed such music?"
"Are these family members plundering my storehouse for themselves to eat?
Having thought this, he rushed toward the gate, crying out at the top of his voice to summon his family members.
At that time, the sounds of music from his household were so chaotic that no one heard the call.
Śakra, hearing the sound of the knocking, said to the people:
"Who is knocking at the door and calling out?"
"You all should cease your music; perhaps that stingy ghost has returned.
When the people heard there was a ghost, they immediately flung open their doors and all fled to escape.

At that time, Luṇḍika came running into the house and saw Śakra surrounded by his retinue, seated in the center; his mother was on his right and his wife on his left. They were adorned with fine garments and beautiful necklaces, amidst the sounds of drums, music, and song, drinking wine at a celebratory gathering, their countenances joyful as they sat in rows.
Lu Zhi was struck with astonishment and asked the Śramaṇa in alarm, "Who are you,
that you come to my house and behave so recklessly?"
Śakra smiled and said,
"Today, my family members have recognized me.
Thereupon, his kinsmen asked Lu-zhi:
"Who are you? Luṣi replied, "I am Luṣi."
The entire family raised their voices in unison and, pointing to Śreṣṭhin, spoke these words:
"This is Lu-zhi; he is the master of our household.
Lu-zhi then immediately asked his family members:
"Who am I now? His family members replied,
"Although you claim to be him, you resemble the ghost Lūji."
Ruci spoke again: "I am not a ghost.
I am Ruci; you all should now observe me well."
Looking back, he spoke to his mother, saying:

"Mother is my mother; my elder brother is my elder brother; my younger brothers are my younger brothers; my wife is the wife whom I revere; my son is the son whom I cherish; and all these attendants are entirely mine."
He then pointed to Śakra and said to his family members:
"This is another person whose countenance resembles mine; he has conjured himself as me.
Since my youth, I have accumulated property, wealth, and treasuries; who is it that has deluded me and dissipated my riches?"
At that time, the members of his household all disbelieved him.
Śākyamuni asked his mother,
"Now, do the two of us look very much alike?"
The mother replied,
"That ghost's appearance is very much like yours.
The mother spoke again to the Śākya:
"Observing your filial piety and service toward me, I truly know you; yet he whom I bore as my son is actually a ghost.
If both of you were equally filial toward me, I would not have been able to distinguish between you."
"Because you are filial and obedient while that man is rebellious and perverse, I know for certain that you are my son.
Turning to the wife, he said, "He is your husband; why do you not now embrace him?"
His wife, feeling ashamed and abashed, spoke these words:
"How strange!
Why do you not extinguish it?"
"I shall never become your wife.
The wife said to Śreṣṭhin, "O Master!"
"I would rather die at your side than ever be born on that demon's side.
Śakra said to the family members:
"If you know for certain that I am Luṭi, why did you let that demon enter before me?"
When the members of his household heard these words, they immediately dragged Lu Zhi’s feet backward, pulling, hauling, and beating him with clubs, driving him out the door.
Arriving in the middle of the lane, he raised his voice and wept bitterly, crying out:
"How strange! How tragic!"
"Now my body, form, and face have become different from what they were; for what reason has my family abandoned me in such a manner?
He then spoke further to those around him:
"Is this body of mine now the same as it was before?"
"Now, is my face as it was before?
Are my speech, my movements, my height, and my physical features different or not?
A bystander said:
"You are as you were before; you are no different from what you previously were.
He then spoke again to the man, saying: "Who am I now?"
"Could it be that you have transformed yourself into another person?
Who, after all, is this name? And where am I now?"
Again, he sighed deeply and said:
"How strange! How marvelous!
What can I possibly say now?"
At that time, Lu-zhi appeared as if he were mad; his other relatives who were not members of his household all came to console him, saying:
"Be careful not to fear!"
"You are Luṭi.
You are currently at the marketplace in the city of Śrāvastī.
We are your kinsmen; therefore, we have come to see you."
"You must strengthen your resolve and devise a plan to clarify the matter for yourself.
When Lu-zhi heard these words, his mind felt somewhat at ease; he wiped away his tears and spoke, further questioning another person:
"Am I truly Lu-zhi or not?"
The others replied,
"You truly are Lu-zhi.
Lu-zhi then said to the crowd:
"Can you all bear witness for me?
The crowd all replied, "We, all of us, shall bear witness for you; it is truly Rūḍhilā."
Luṣi replied: "If that is so, listen as I explain the circumstances in detail:
'Who is there among the young men who bears such a striking resemblance to me?'"
Sitting on the same bed with my beloved wife, knees touching knees,
my own dear kinsmen saw me beaten and drove me out;
yet those very kinsmen who loved him so now dwell peacefully within my home.
I endured the sufferings of hunger and cold to accumulate various wealth and treasures;
yet now he uses them at his own will, while I have not a single hair’s breadth of a share.
He is like Vaiśravaṇa, indulging himself in food and clothing as he pleases.
The people within the city, each harboring doubts and wonder,
all spoke these words:
"How should this matter be understood?"
Among them was one of clear wisdom who spoke these words:
"This person here is a deceitful man whose physical appearance resembles Lu-zhi;
knowing him to be exceedingly stingy and greedy, he has come to disturb and trouble him."
"We have all witnessed your deliverance together; it is not fitting that we should abandon you so easily.
When the people heard these words, they were all of one mind and said: "Luti!..."
"What is your intention now?
What do you wish to do?
At that moment, Lu-zhi spoke these words:
"You all must assemble for my sake; tomorrow we shall go together to the king's presence.
All the people said, "Tomorrow we shall escort you to the king's presence."
When the next day arrived, the people said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Now is precisely the right time.
Lu-zhi then said,
"This is a momentous matter."
"I have no mastery over my own wealth; if you can lend me some money, should I obtain it, I shall repay you.
All the people said, "Whatever you require, we shall provide to you."
He asked again,
"What do you require?
At that time, the elder Lu-zhi replied:
"Now, give me two pieces of cotton cloth worth four *zhu* of gold, and I shall present them to the king.
Everyone laughed and thought to themselves:
"Lu-zhi has never done such a thing before; to speak of 'four *zhu*' is truly a great gift!"
At that time, Lu-zhi took up two pieces of fine cotton cloth and went to the king’s gate, where he said to the gatekeeper:
"I now wish to present an offering."
At that time, the gatekeeper was greatly astonished and laughed, saying:
"In thirty years, I have never heard of him coming to the gate to offer a contribution; how is it that today he is suddenly able to do so?"
Then the gatekeeper immediately entered and informed the king, joining his palms and saying:
"It is unprecedented!
Lu Zhi-jin is here at the gate, wishing to present an offering."
The king’s mind was grave and reflective; he did not immediately give way to anger or joy, but thought to himself:
"Today it cannot be because of a festival that these people have come to my gate. Rudrāyaṇa is miserly, so he too should not have come to my door.
Nor should the gatekeepers be playing a joke upon me."
What do you think?
I cannot believe it.
As for one who is a king, he is like the great ocean which does not reject even a small stream; how could one possibly calculate the amount of his wealth?
The king then immediately granted him entrance.
The king thought to himself:
"This Luṭi is by nature miserly; how could he suddenly become like this, as if he were not about to die?"

Immediately, Luṇḍika went with the crowd to the king’s presence, intending to take out the two cotton cloths to present them to the king. As he pulled at the cloths, they were held tightly under his armpits; he could not pull them free. He turned around and pulled with all his might and great effort until he finally managed to get them out.
Once he had emerged, Śakra immediately manifested two bundles of grass.
Upon seeing the bundles of grass, he was struck with great shame and sat down upon the ground.
When the King saw this, he felt compassion and spoke to him, saying:
"Even if you were bound in a bundle of straw, you would suffer no pain; whatever you wish to say, speak according to your own will.
Lu-zhi, choked with grief and sobbing, said:
"Upon seeing this grass, my shame is so profound that I cannot sink my body into the earth."
"I do not know whether this body now exists or does not exist;
what can I possibly say?
When the king heard these words, he felt a special sense of compassion and asked those nearby:
"He is now choked with grief and unable to speak.
If you know his intention, you should speak on his behalf.
A bystander replied to the king:

"As for why Lu Zhi has come today to address Your Majesty: I do not know who this person is, though his appearance resembles Lu Zhi's. When he went to his home, he falsely claimed to be Lu Zhi and was able to cause the family members to develop an affection for him.

He squandered their wealth until it was entirely exhausted, leading the family to lose all sense of recognition; they drove him out, treating him like a stranger on the road. For this reason, his heart is filled with anguish, and he is unable to speak."
The King said: "If it is so, then this is indeed a cause for suffering. Why is that?
"My own property has been used by another.
Even though this is so, I shall resolve the matter so that he may have his household wealth returned.
The king spoke again, saying:
"Though people of the world may resemble one another in physical form, their minds and intentions are not necessarily identical;
though they may resemble one another in mind, there are secret matters in the hidden parts of their bodies that they may not know of each other, and thus there must be some slight difference."
"Do not grieve; I shall now conduct a thorough investigation for you.
At that time, there was a minister named Sostiu (宿舊) who rose, joined his palms, and addressed the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
"The wisdom and compassionate mercy of Your Majesty toward the wronged ought indeed to be thus.
At that time, an elder spoke these verses:
"For those who are afflicted by sorrow, suffering, and fear, The King provides protection and refuge."
Toward those who are poor and in distress, the king should act as a close friend;
toward those who practice the true and the good, the king should be a companion in the Dharma;
and toward those who engage in evil deeds, the king should serve as an elephant-hook.
At that time, Lu-zhi prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and addressed the king, saying:
"As for the place where my family’s hidden stores of wealth and treasures are kept, he will ultimately never be able to know its location;
as for my own private matters, how could he possibly know them?"
"I only pray that Your Majesty will investigate this for me!
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon the man who resembled Rudrāyaṇa, commanding him to come quickly.
He was summoned and arrived at the king's presence, standing to one side.
The king could not distinguish between the two figures.
He observed them closely and was struck by a sense of wonder, thinking:

"Their age and appearance, the size of their bodies, their faces, speech, smiles, and complexions are all identical; they are like those created by illusion, exactly the same with no difference whatsoever."
"Now these two persons stand before me, indistinguishable from one another, causing me great alarm and doubt.
The king asked the one who had been summoned, "Who are you?"
He then sighed to himself and said:
"My life now is lived in vain; it would be better for me to die.
How is it that though I have grown up in a royal kingdom, I am not recognized by the king?"
He then asked me,
"Who is your name?
The prince felt a slight sense of shame and embarrassment.
"This is indeed Ruci," he said to the one before him,
"What further do you wish to discuss?"
Ruci replied, "I am Ruci; he is not.
The king said:
"You two now resemble images in a mirror; your complexions and features are identical. How can you be distinguished?
Lu-zhi replied, "For this reason, I first took refuge in the King.
Whenever there is anyone suffering from illness, facing calamity, or in urgent distress and fear, they all take refuge in the King."
The king said, "It is indeed so;
it is precisely for this purpose that I receive taxes from the people.
After reflecting briefly, he spoke to Śakra, saying:
"I wish to ask you: Luṭi is by nature stingy and greedy, whereas you are fond of giving alms; since your dispositions are so different, how can you now say that this is Luṭi?"
Śakra replied: "Your Majesty should indeed ask such a subtle question.
It is truly as Your Majesty says; nevertheless, I have personally received instruction from the Buddha:"

Those who are stingy and greedy fall among the hungry ghosts (preta), where for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years they suffer the pains of hunger and thirst; though they seek pus, blood, excrement, urine, and other impurities, they ultimately cannot obtain even as much as a hair's breadth, while clear, cool rivers and springs turn into flowing fire.

Having heard that stinginess and greed possess such faults and are causes for fear, and desiring to abandon this evil, I immediately relinquish stinginess for this reason, and the mind of generosity arises.
The King said:
"Truly there is this principle; just as a soiled garment becomes clean when washed with ash, the mind defiled by afflictions is cleared away upon hearing the Dharma.
The King then spoke to his ministers:
"How can one know which of these two persons is Lu-zhi and which is not?
An elder replied:
"Ask him about all the secret matters within his household; if there are points of agreement or discrepancy, only then can it be known.
The king said, "My affairs are numerous and pressing; I cannot question him in detail."
"What you have said is correct; it should be asked in this manner.
He then separated the two men, placing each in a different location, and questioned them, saying:

"Regarding your current internal and external relatives—their ages, their number, and their names—as well as all the houses, doors, and wealth within your homes, including everything in your treasuries and all the various items upon and beneath the earth, each of you must record these yourselves and prepare clear written accounts, which you shall bring here immediately."
Then these two men each arrived carrying their letters; all the secret matters and the handwriting were identical in every respect.
When the king saw this, he was struck with the thought that such a thing had never occurred before:
"Even as I now exhaust my mental faculties and employ every kind of deliberation, I am unable to distinguish between them."
"This is not a human matter; it must be the work of a non-human being.
The king said, "Go and summon these two men to come before me."
After the king had gazed at him for a long time, he said to his attendants,
"Call her mother here.
They immediately summoned the mother.
Having arrived, she paid her respects to the king. The king joined his palms and said, "I, too, revere the elderly.
The old woman replied:
“May Your Majesty live ten thousand years, be free from all enmity and harm, and cultivate merit without weariness!
The king commanded a seat to be spread and bade the old woman sit.
The king then spoke to her, saying:
"Now, between these two men, who is your son and who is not your son?
Śakra spoke these secret words to his mother:
"May you not again be made to experience suffering as before.
The mother said,
"My son, do not grieve."
The old woman respectfully addressed the king, saying:
"This boy is compassionate and filial; he has provided me with all manner of offerings and has been obedient to me, so he is my son.
That one was neither respectful nor filial, and he never showed me any affection or love; I know he is not my son."
"Although these two men know the difference between good and bad, their voices are so similar that even I cannot distinguish them.
The king asked again,
"I wish to ask you about another matter."
"When you raised this child from infancy, including during his baths, did you ever see any hidden parts of his body, such as scars, moles, or private marks? Do you remember them?"
The mother replied,
"There is. Śakra reflected:
"I shall now act exactly as my mother did.
At that time, Śakra listened intently to his mother’s words.
His mother said to the king:
"My son has a scar the size of a small bean beneath his left rib.
Śakra thought to himself:
"Even if there were a scar as large as Mount Sumeru, I could create it; how much more so this tiny scar?"
He then manifested a transformation.
The king thought to himself:
"Now that I have adjudicated this matter, I shall surely attain certainty."
The king said, "Each of you,
expose your left armpits and raise your arms high.
Once they had raised their arms, he saw that the two scars were no different from one another.
The king and his ministers laughed aloud and spoke these words:
"A matter such as this has never been heard or seen; it can cause people to laugh, it can cause people to fear, and it can cause people to doubt. This is a marvelous thing, truly terrifying."
The King said to his ministers:
"Matters such as these are not within my capacity to resolve.
We must take these two men to the Jetavana, to where the Buddha resides; there they will surely obtain a definitive resolution."
"You have interrupted the joy of this festive gathering of ours.
At that time, the king spoke these verses:
"The Sun of the Buddha has long since risen, Able to rescue and deliver the world."
Liberated from all faults and evils, he has dried up the ocean of craving and desire.
His face is like the full moon; endowed with supernormal powers and the divine eye, he is honored and sustained by all throughout the three realms, sovereign over all things.
“The Greatly Compassionate One will surely be able to eliminate our doubts;
everyone praises this, saying it is most excellent.

Having spoken these verses, the king and his ministers each adorned themselves with celestial crowns and upper garments, their bodies embellished with pearls and necklaces. Holding fragrant flowers, they followed behind the king, each placing one of the two Luṭis upon an elephant, which were likewise decorated in various ways.

At that time, the king himself mounted a carriage adorned with feathered ornaments, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of kinds of musical performances, and followed behind the king to the Jetavana. There, he set aside his five royal insignia—the celestial crown, the precious parasol, the sword, the sandals, and the mani-jewel—and, having adjusted his appearance and demeanor, proceeded to where the Buddha was.
“At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, as well as the fourfold assembly.
The king and the great multitude prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to the Buddha; having risen, they joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘I and all those in the triple world are shrouded in ignorance and darkness, unable to distinguish the true from the false; only the Buddha’s mind is pure.’”
All sentient beings are scorched by hundreds of thousands of afflictions, yet only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, brings them peace and extinguishes them;
all in the world are bound by birth and death, yet only the Buddha alone has attained liberation and acts as a true kinsman and friend to all sentient beings;
for all who are blind and ignorant, the Buddha serves as their eyes.
"By various causes and conditions, we were unable to distinguish between these two men as to which was Lu-ji and which was not Lu-ji.
Having brought the two Lu-jis before the Buddha, they said: [They presented them before the Buddha.]
All the people sat in silence, each in their place.
The transformed Lu-ji, his countenance serene and joyful, adorned his body with various ornaments and necklaces, and sat in silence.
The true Rudrāyaṇa was haggard in appearance, wearing soiled and greasy clothes, with dust covering his body; overcome by extreme sorrow and suffering, he spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, you possess great compassion and rescue all beings; I pray that you will rescue me!"
At that time, Śakra, seeing his distress and dejection, smiled to himself.
King Prasenajit rose from his seat, joined his palms, and asked the Buddha:
"In this matter, the Buddha is able to bear witness and know."
All sentient beings are shrouded in darkness by afflictions; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, holds aloft the torch of wisdom to guide all beings along the path to liberation.

Like a great king of physicians, and like a guide, he is able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings and grant them the wealth of roots of goodness. Because he destroys and annihilates the fetters and latent tendencies, he is called the Great Sage (Maharṣi).
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
I pray that you will use the fire of wisdom to burn away the dense forest of my afflictions and the web of doubt.
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will sever our doubts:
between these two people now, who is right and who is wrong?
At that time, the World-Honored One raised his hand, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and spoke to Śakra, saying:

"What have you done? Śakra immediately extinguished Luṭi’s physical form and restored his original appearance, which was adorned with various radiances. Adorning his body with wish-fulfilling jewels and necklaces, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"Constantly subdued by stinginess, I was unwilling to provide food or clothing for myself."
With five coins' worth of wine and parched grain, he added salt and drank it;
having drunk it, he became greatly intoxicated, and while laughing, singing, and dancing,
he reviled us gods with insults.
"For this reason, I am thus distressed.
The Buddha said to Śakra:
"All sentient beings have faults and transgressions; you should let them go."
At that time, Lu-zhi said to Śakra:
"All this wealth and property that I have accumulated with such great hardship—will you not use my riches until they are exhausted?"
Śakra said, "I have not damaged even a single hair’s breadth of your wealth.
The Buddha said to Luṭi:
"Return to your home and look at your wealth.
Lu-zhi said, "All the wealth I possess has already been exhausted; what would be the use of returning home?"
Śakra said, "I have not diminished your wealth by even a hair's breadth. Lu-zhi replied:
"I do not believe you; I believe only the words of the Buddha.
Because he believed the words of the Buddha, he immediately attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.

At that time, the eight classes of devas and dragons, as well as the fourfold assembly, having seen and heard this, attained the fruits of the four paths and planted the causes and conditions for the three types of karma.
The various devas and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, departed with joy.
*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Elder Luṭi*.
